title: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine

Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine

Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine

                WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 05: First lady Melania Trump gives hand written letters to Russian special envoy and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund Kirill Dmitrievon (L) and Ukrainian human rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets (C) to deliver to their presidents during an event on a temporary Russia-Ukraine ceasefire at the White House on November 5, 2026 in Washington, DC.
                
                    Samuel Corum/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Samuel Corum/Getty Images
    

   
   First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine.   The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.   "We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."   Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.   
   The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.   The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.   Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.   "On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.   Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.   "I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."   The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.   President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.   Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.   
   "It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."   Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.   "In this White House ceremony, we were honoring the Russians that were the cause of both the occupation of Oleshky, the starvation of Oleshky, and now we're honoring them for allowing aid to come into Oleshky," said Conley, who is now a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. "The more we create this equivalency where the Russians and the Ukrainians are equal in this crisis, it is putting this thing upside down."

body:
Loading... 
   Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.   A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes. That's normal and expected.   Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press:   
    Loading... 
   In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.     Loading...

title: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row
description: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row   California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sente
body:
Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row   California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.

    
        Politics
    


      
            
                  
            November 5, 20266:11 PM ET
         
      
       From
   
   
                              By                
            


      
      CA Death Row Cleared
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6030961/nx-s1-9993873" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    




      California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.   


    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  California Governor Gavin Newsom announced today that he is commuting all 548 death sentences on the books in his state. He is reducing all of the sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The governor says California's death row is the largest in the Western hemisphere. Now, this action comes during a renewed national debate about capital punishment, following the recent botched execution attempt of a woman convicted of murder in Tennessee and also following the Trump administration's talk of livestreaming an execution at Fort Hood. That proposal was later rejected by President Trump. Scott Shafer of member station KQED is following the California governor's action today and joins us now. Hi, Scott.SCOTT SHAFER, BYLINE: Hey, Ailsa.CHANG: OK, so how did Governor Newsom explain his reasons for taking this step?SHAFER: Well, the governor has been thinking about this for a long time now. He signaled on his podcast last month that he was framing it as a rocking chair test, meaning - how would he feel when he's old and sitting in a rocking chair reflecting on his life? He clearly sees opposition to the death penalty as, you know, kind of fundamental to his values and his faith. So it was pretty clear this was going to happen. They waited until just after the election to do it. He issued a statement today explaining why he did this, and among other things, he said the death penalty is a failure. You know, we haven't had an execution in California in 20 years. He also said it's immoral for the state to murder somebody and that it isn't applied fairly anyway.CHANG: OK. Well, Newsom had already put death sentences on hold, right? So explain how this step today differs from that earlier step.SHAFER: Yeah, he issued that moratorium on executions two months after he became governor - that was 2019 - dismantled the execution chamber at San Quentin prison, and they moved death row inmates from San Quentin to other maximum-security prisons across the state. So in some ways, this is symbolic since there aren't any executions on the horizon anyway. But by commuting these hundreds of sentences, it might give momentum to death penalty opponents in other states, you know, to lobby governors there to do something similar. And I should emphasize, Ailsa, that Newsom's actions today do not eliminate the death penalty in California. Only the voters can do that.CHANG: Right. OK, so what's been the reaction so far there in California? Like, what have victims had to say about this?SHAFER: Well, Newsom met with many crime victims before he issued the moratorium on executions back in 2019. Needless to say, those are very hard conversations, very raw. He met with many of those folks again over the past months as he considered this decision, and in his statement today, he sort of spoke to them saying, commuting these death sentences could resurface excruciating memories for them. He does not dismiss that in any way. He also said that he didn't want to pick and choose which death sentences to commute and which to let stand, saying that that could inadvertently create two classes of murder victims, which he did not want to do.CHANG: OK. Well, you suggest that today's actions by Newsom were pretty anticipated. I mean, Newsom is often mentioned as a possible candidate for president in 2028. So talk about the political context here for this move.SHAFER: Yeah, this was anticipated, for those of us paying attention to it. He waited until after Tuesday's election, so it wouldn't become an issue. And as to the politics, you know, there are certainly some advisers in Newsom's political orbit who urged him not to do it as he gets ready to run for president. But one of his advisers said that when he did this seven years ago, Newsom never asked to see any polls or look at anything related to the politics of it. And across the country, Gallup has been polling on this for decades, and support for the death penalty is at its lowest point in decades. So it's not really clear Newsom will pay a political price for this.CHANG: That is Scott Shafer from member station KQED in San Francisco. Thank you, Scott.SHAFER: Thank you.

title: A judge blocks construction of Trump's arch moments after it won federal approval
description: Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle t
body:
Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle to protest President Trump's proposed arch on Thursday night as a federal panel heard hours of testimony from concerned citizens. It voted to approve the structure.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.    Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia.   She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion, in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.   
   Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.    "The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.    Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.   The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.   A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.   Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.    
   Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.   The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.   Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.   
   Among their many concerns, critics said the structure would obstruct an important view, insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.   Many see the arch as part of Trump's unilateral effort to memorialize himself in the nation's capital — and described Democrats' midterm sweep as a referendum against it.   "Leaving aside all of the legitimate concerns and challenges about the required approvals, funding, land use, single-source bidding, and peer review, the American people spoke this past Tuesday at the ballot box," said former D.C. resident Emi Yamauchi. "They said enough vanity projects, enough corruption, enough Reflecting Pool travesties."   Only a handful of speakers offered support for the arch, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both of whom are veterans.   Much of the night's testimony was heartfelt and personal: Many speakers had family members buried — or plans for their own future burials — at Arlington National Cemetery. Several implored the commissioners not to ruin their reputations by recording their support for the arch.   
   "[These are] warnings about the threat your own behavior poses to your political power, your moral authority, the legacy you leave to your descendants, and your eternal souls," said Stephen Eubank, some seven hours into the public testimony.   
   As the night wore on, a few speakers even questioned whether the commissioners — who were not shown on screen — were even listening. Many suggested the approval was a foregone conclusion, noting the political makeup of the commission and the fact that Trump-appointed Chair Mark Paoletta and several other members had expressed their support for the arch at the start of the meeting.   The commission started deliberating just before 10 p.m. The discussion lasted less than an hour.   The commissioners who spoke first were Trump allies and appointees. They thanked the speakers for taking the time to share their views, but — in brief comments — expressed their support for moving forward. They continued to cast the arch as a tribute to the nation and those who served, despite the broad pushback from individual veterans and veterans' groups.   The Trump allies dismissed concerns that the arch would violate D.C.'s restrictions on building heights as well as federal environmental and historic preservation laws. They maintained that Congress authorized the project when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle in 1925, which were never built.   And they pointed to recent claims by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that the monument will enhance national security — even though officials at the meeting confirmed that no such analysis or details were included in the final submission. In fact, Interior Department official Greg Wischer said "specific national security functions have been filed under seal" in court but that the National Park Service "has not been privy to any national defense preparations."   The most vocal criticism of the arch came from D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, a Democrat who sits on the council. He asked questions about the arch's purpose — military and otherwise — earlier in the meeting and said, during deliberations, that he was dissatisfied with the government's contradictory answers.   
   "We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plan," Mendelson said. He introduced a motion to postpone the vote until those plans could be submitted, or until the commission's next meeting in early December. The motion failed by a vote of 4 to 8.   Vice Chair Stuart Levenbach, a Trump appointee, expressed concerns about delaying the vote because the "project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today," suggesting the government wants to "commence building very quickly."   Within minutes, the commission had given the arch its green light. The Trump administration notified the court within half an hour. By Friday, that light had turned red — at least temporarily.    "While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump Administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project,"  Rep. Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said in a statement.    Arch critics look to the courts and Congress for relief    Historic preservation groups wasted no time slamming both the process and the outcome.   Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, called the night's vote a "sham."   "It undermines the democratic process, violates federal statute, and insults our nation's veterans who have made the ultimate sacrifice," he said in a statement. "From the start, this Arch project has been driven by an artificial sense of urgency, while public opposition has been brushed aside."   Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager for the National Parks Conservation Association, said in a statement that the organization is disappointed but not surprised. He vowed to "bring this to members of Congress, to ensure this arch is never built. Not here. Not ever."   
   Many Democratic lawmakers have vowed to stop — and investigate — the arch after they regain a Congressional majority in January.   Robert Weissman, the co-president of Public Citizen — the consumer rights nonprofit representing the veterans in their lawsuit — told NPR on Thursday that Congress doesn't need to act to stop the arch, since it never actively approved it. That decision, he said, will be up to the courts.   But, he added: "It would be fine if Congress takes additional measures to block construction, since we've seen this lawless administration circumvent the law and court orders so frequently."   Virginia Rep. Don Beyer has introduced a bill that would prohibit and defund the arch, and said Thursday he expects the number of co-sponsors to grow from 80 to at least 200 in the new year.   And Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., the ranking Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners that companies and "officials working to advance a project not authorized by Congress will put themselves at legal risk."   He argued that the project violates federal environmental and historic preservation laws, which fall within the jurisdiction of the House committee he expects to soon lead.   "I urge all officials and firms involved with this illegal project to consider the legal hazards they may be facing by advancing it, because, in case you hadn't heard, we'll soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously," Huffman said.

title: 'He's got to go': Hakeem Jeffries calls for Hegseth's removal but stops short of impeachment
description: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D
body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., at a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4.
                
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
    

   
   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House, says his party will push to end the war in Iran and hold Trump administration officials accountable after its midterm victories. But how far Democrats will go remains unclear.   Speaking with Morning Edition on Friday, Jeffries called the conflict a "war of choice" that "has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices and fertilizer prices," raising the cost of everyday goods.   He said Democrats "shouldn't have to wait" for the new Congress to act.    But with majorities in both chambers, Jeffries said Democrats could pass a war powers resolution to try and force President Trump to end the war. If passed, it would present President Trump with the choice to either sign or veto it. Overriding a veto would require two-thirds majorities in both chambers. As of now, Democrats are short of a veto-proof majority in both chambers.   
   Jeffries stopped short of supporting impeachment proceedings against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.   Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns.   "We'll have that conversation," Jeffries said, calling Hegseth "the most unqualified secretary of defense in American history."   Asked directly whether Hegseth should be impeached, Jeffries said, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus."   "He's got to go," he added.   Jeffries said the House Judiciary and Oversight committees would investigate alleged wrongdoing by the Trump administration.   Asked about voters calling for new Democratic leadership, including the next House speaker, Jeffries said the decision rests with the House Democratic Caucus. He defended Democrats' record, saying they had "battled Trump on every issue up until this point and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago."   Listen to the full interview using the blue button above, or read the transcript below, lightly edited for length and clarity.   Leila Fadel: The person expected to be the next House Speaker and its first Black Speaker is the current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and he joins me now to talk about what that will look like. So your party has a real mandate here in Congress, and it comes with expectations from voters that you'll make life more affordable. What is at the top of your agenda if you're elected House Speaker?   House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries: Well, it was a tremendous victory for the American people and a strong rebuke of MAGA extremism, which has made life more expensive for everyday Americans. Despite their promises to lower the high cost of living on day one. There are several steps that we can take to create a more comfortable way of life for the American people, including ending the war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed gas prices, diesel prices, and fertilizer prices, and as a result, increased the cost of groceries and everyday goods on the American people.   
   Leila Fadel: How will you know?   Jeffries: Well, we shouldn't have to wait till the new Congress until that happens. The American people have clearly spoken. Even the Vice President has expressed an understanding that it's time to end the war, or Republicans will continue to pay electoral consequences in that regard, but in the majority, having both the House and the Senate, we can advance strong war powers resolutions that the president will have to take up, get it to his desk, and then explain himself to the American people if, in fact, he decides to use his veto pen.   Fadel: Do you think he'll be willing to work with you on this? I mean, he's given some mixed messages, saying I'm ready to work with the Democrats, but I'll also be "Mr. Veto."   Jeffries: I think it's incredibly important, and that we all listen to what has been expressed by the American people throughout this campaign. We promised that we were going to relentlessly fight for a more affordable America, work to drive down the high price of groceries and gas and housing, fight to make health care affordable for every single American, and at the same period of time hold the crooks accountable for all of the corruption that has been visited upon the American people. And there's an economic cost to corruption that clearly the American people have concluded Republicans have visited upon them. So hopefully, all of my colleagues on the other side of the aisle, as a result of the roaring voices of the American people, will conclude that we should decisively act to make the lives of the American people affordable.   Fadel: I want to ask about a pressing matter. Republican Congressman and Trump critic Thomas Massie of Kentucky says he'll force a vote on the House floor of eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth if he does not resign. Here's what Hegseth said in response in a video posted online:   "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me".    Will you and other Democrats vote to impeach if this happens?   Jeffries: We'll have that conversation. We'll have that conversation when we gather as a caucus immediately upon our return, but I've been very clear about my position with respect to Pete Hegseth. He's the most unqualified Secretary of Defense in American history. He should never have been confirmed by Senate Republicans, and we've seen all the damage that he's visited upon the American people, the world, and the Pentagon in terms of military readiness, and so I first called for Pete Hegseth to be fired by Donald Trump in the spring of 2025. I have not changed my position, and he should have resigned or been fired a long time ago. But certainly in the immediate aftermath of the stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism that the American people visited at the polls a few days ago,   
   Fadel: But is this the way? Should he be impeached?   Jeffries: Well, as I indicated, we'll have that conversation as a caucus together, and I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus, but I've been very strong and clear in my opinions as it relates to Pete Hegseth. He's got to go.   Fadel: You said yesterday that Americans don't want Democrats to get even; they want you to get things done on their behalf, specifically around affordability. Now, Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming Oversight Committee Chair, struck a very different tone. He posted online, "Lawyer up," and laid out a plan that included investigating the Trump family for possible crimes in the next Congress. Are you on the same page when it comes to accountability?   Jeffries: Yeah. Well, we've repeatedly made clear over the last two years is that we've got to relentlessly make life more affordable for the American people, while at the same period of time, visit accountability on those who have been engaged in law breaking, norm breaking, and unleashing unprecedented corruption on the American people. And so, it's my expectation, and we're working closely, of course, with Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee and Democrats on the Oversight Committee, who will lead our accountability efforts, along with all of the relevant committees across the Congress, because the levels of corruption have been unprecedented, and we've made clear to the American people that if you have folks out there who have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people, or screwing over the American people, we're going to hold the crooks accountable. We're going to function like a separate and co-equal branch of government, as opposed to, unfortunately, what my Republican colleagues have done is to bury their heads in the sand and be nothing more than a reckless rubber stamp for Donald Trump's extreme agenda. So we got to follow the facts. We got to apply the law. We got to be guided by the Constitution, and we have to deliver a government of the people, by the people, and for the people.   
   Fadel: Now, your party had a historic win this week, but we were out across the country speaking to people, and at the same time as choosing your candidates, voters were expressing dissatisfaction with the party leadership, and what they saw as an inability to stand up to Trump meaningfully. In the last two years, they wanted new blood in the party. They said they want completely new leadership of the party. That includes for a future speaker of the House. What do you say to the voters who are skeptical of Democratic establishment leaders like yourself?   Jeffries: Well, we're going to put it into the hands of the House Democratic Caucus as we chart a path forward. But we've battled Trump on every issue up until this point, and then just decisively defeated him a few days ago.   The digital version was edited by Treye Green and Jason Breslow.

title: What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina
description: Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave i
body:
Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:  To North Carolina now, where Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats. That's according to race calls by The Associated Press. Democrats also held on to a redistricted seat. Most of those races, they were not even considered competitive going into Tuesday's election. The remaining congressional races in the state are still too close to call. The surprising results were just one part of the big blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times. Colin Campbell covers politics for member station WUNC. He's on the line from Raleigh. Hey there, Colin.COLIN CAMPBELL, BYLINE: Hey, Mary Louise.KELLY: OK, tell me more about North Carolina's congressional map.CAMPBELL: So Republicans currently hold 10 of the state's 14 House seats, and last year, state lawmakers gerrymandered those maps even more to try to unseat Democrat Don Davis in the state's northeastern corner. That didn't actually happen. AP called that race for Davis today. It was one of the most expensive races in the country and one we'd all been watching along with the western North Carolina district where Democrat Jamie Ager flipped an open GOP seat by a pretty big margin.But most of us weren't paying close attention at all to the nine districts with Republican incumbents on the ballot. All of them won by big margins two years ago, but we learned today that Congressman Tim Moore, Richard Hudson, Brad Knott and Addison McDowell all lost their seats to little-known Democrats. Hudson's particularly notable because he's actually the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. That's the campaign operation for the House GOP.KELLY: And then there are four other Republican incumbents in North Carolina's delegation. Where do things stand for them?CAMPBELL: None of their races have been called just yet. Three have narrow leads, but the state is still in the process of counting provisional and absentee ballots, so those numbers could change. Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx is currently just 99 votes behind her Democratic opponent. She's been in office since 2005, also chairs the House Rules Committee. All four of those races could be headed to recounts, and under our state law here, that process won't actually start until after November 13.KELLY: So next week. So, you know, the question we've been asking for a couple of days now has been - how did Republicans manage to do so poorly? We're asking that in a lot of states. My question to you - how did Republicans do so poorly in a state where they had effectively drawn the map to favor their party?CAMPBELL: A lot of it is the national environment. They just weren't expecting this big of a wave when they drew these maps and tried to figure out the optimal number. But North Carolina's U.S. Senate race also played a role. Former Governor Roy Cooper had such a big polling lead in that race that national Republican groups pulled all of their advertising for their candidate, Michael Whatley, moved that money to other states like Kansas in the final weeks. Most of the other Republicans here were actually relying on that spending to drive voter turnout in their races, and some of the congressional incumbents started running their own TV ads just in the final weeks of the campaign but looks like that was too little too late. Whatley ended up with less than 40% of the vote. He was Trump's pick to run for the seat but never really won over the Republican base here.KELLY: Other things we should know about how the Blue wave broke there in North Carolina?CAMPBELL: Democrats here easily won the state for the state Supreme Court, and they won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2008. They're pretty close to a tie in the state Senate too, which, if that happens, would be broken by the lieutenant governor who happens to be a Democrat. That's going to give Democratic Governor Josh Stein a lot more power next year, and he wants to make some redistricting reforms. Republicans, of course, still have some influence. So yesterday, he called on the two parties to come together and work on the affordability issues that dominated the election.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)JOSH STEIN: What the voters want us to do is listen to what happened last night and focus on that. They want us to work for them and not be focused on reflecting pools or ballrooms or triumphal arches. They want a government that is worrying about their lives, the fact that gas has shot through the roof in price, that electricity bills are going up.KELLY: All right, Democratic Governor Josh Stein in that reporting there from Colin Campbell, who covers North Carolina politics for member station WUNC. Thank you, Colin.CAMPBELL: Thanks.(SOUNDBITE OF DIXSON SONG, "LA NOCTURNE")

title: Judge halts construction of Trump's arch. And, Labor Department to release jobs report
description: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   Rising prices and stagnant wages fueled frustration during this week's midterm elections, prompting voters to express their discontent at the ballot box. Similarly, the stock market experienced a downturn yesterday. Concerns about a Democratic Congress regulating AI led to a more than 5% drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq, wiping out more than $2 trillion in market value. This decline followed from Wednesday when shares rose as investors were relieved that the midterms had made Congress's fate clear. In contrast, there has been less volatility in the job market, and today the Labor Department is set to release the latest jobs report.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Stocks sank as investors fear an incoming Democratic Congress — and states across the country — could crack down on the AI industry and data centers.
                
                    TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
    

   
   🎧 Today's jobs report is expected to show that employers added about 60,000 jobs last month, NPR's Scott Horsley tells Up First. While this isn't robust growth, it should keep the unemployment rate low. As long as the job market stays stable, the Federal Reserve can focus on fighting stubbornly high inflation, which likely drove the recent election outcomes.   A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of President Trump's 250-foot arch in the capital. District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order just before midnight Friday, halting work for 14 days at the request of D.C. and Virginia governments. In her 33-page opinion, she scrutinized the administration's justifications for the arch, particularly its focus on national security and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The arch is planned for Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.   
   🎧 The judges' decision followed a contentious meeting last night, during which the National Capital Planning Commission, filled with Trump allies, voted to approve the arch, NPR's Rachel Treisman says. The commission's approval came despite significant opposition to the arch from dozens and dozens of people. After nearly nine hours, the panel gave the go-ahead, which would have allowed excavation to begin. Several Democratic lawmakers are already talking about blocking the arch. Democrat Jared Huffman of California, likely to become head of the House Natural Resources Committee, warned commissioners at yesterday's meeting that anyone advancing projects not authorized by Congress risks legal repercussions.   School enrollment is set to plunge by another 2 million kids by 2030, and education experts say the crisis will be worsened by the deportation of immigrant families with school-age children. Even before the Trump administration's policy changes, public schools faced a significant decline due to shrinking family sizes. U.S. Census data show the number of children under 18 nationwide had fallen by about 2.1 million since 2010. The Trump administration's large-scale deportations began after public schools started facing a demographic crisis, with a Migration Policy Institute study indicating that 1.9 million people left the U.S. during Trump's second term. This situation marks the first time in nearly a century that birth rates and immigration levels are both low at the same time.   
   Harmeet Dhillon has left her position as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division after 18 tumultuous months. During her time in the role, she transformed the unit, saw a significant loss of career staff and aggressively pursued Trump's agenda. She is the first senior official to depart since Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterms. Dhillon called the role "the honor of a lifetime."   Healthy or hype?   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Father and son holding toothbrushes and toothpaste in a bathroom, sharing a relaxed morning oral care routine together.
                
                    mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images
    

   
   Healthy or Hype? is an NPR series helping readers and listeners sort truth from fiction when it comes to online health claims.   Many people are replacing their fluoride dental products with those containing hydroxyapatite. It is a mineral that boasts cavity protection, whitening and enamel strengthening — all without fluoride. While health experts widely agree that fluoride is beneficial to health, interest in fluoride-free alternatives is growing. A driving force behind the trend is Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. blaming water fluoridation for health issues like arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer and neurodevelopmental disorders. Here's what dentists say about it.   🪥 Fluoride has been extensively researched, especially in long-term studies, but early research on hydroxyapatite shows promising results.🪥 For patients considering both options, Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio, recommends using fluoride because there is more evidence supporting its effectiveness.🪥 Amaechi was an author of a 2021 study in Scientific Reports that followed 177 children for a year and compared hydroxyapatite and fluoride toothpaste. The findings showed similar outcomes of tooth decay in both groups.🪥 The American Dental Association told NPR that it acknowledges that more people are using hydroxyapatite products, which may aid in remineralization. However, they noted that research on its clinical effectiveness is still limited and unclear.🪥 The ADA recommends brushing teeth twice daily for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, flossing every day and visiting a dentist regularly.   
   Weekend picks   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                James Spader as Ultron and Paul Bettany as Vision in VisionQuest.
                
                    Marvel
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Marvel
    

   
   Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:   🍿 Movies: John Turturro stars as Harry, a skilled pickpocket and caretaker for his wife, in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York. His life changes dramatically when he steals a backpack from a college kid, only to discover he is the grandson of a crime boss.   📺 TV: VisionQuest is Marvel's finale series to the trilogy that started with WandaVision and continued through Agatha All Along. It serves as a timely parable about artificial intelligence, while also exploring themes of daddy issues, according to Pop Culture Happy Hour.   📚 Books: As it gets cooler, it's the perfect time to cozy up with a good book. Here are six must-read November releases, featuring tales of star-crossed romance, hard-won redemption and high-stakes struggles.   🎵 Music: As 2026 draws to a close, NPR's All Songs Considered revisits some great songs from earlier in the year that might have been missed, including Northern Iowa's pop artist Kinji and Mexican singer Silvana Estrada.   🎮 Gaming: Nintendo's Ocarina of Time remake secures its legacy in gaming, but despite its high production values, NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino says it left him feeling oddly bereft.   ❓ Quiz: The midterms are over, and while this week was politics-heavy, that's not all that happened. This quiz offers a great recap of the week's diverse events.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Somali school girls play football during lunch break at the Howlwadag Primary School in Howlwadag District, south of Mogadishu. on October, 5, 2016.
                
                    Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images
    

   
   New global data suggest only a small minority of kids and teens get at least one hour a day of exercise that breaks a sweat, as recommended by the World Health Organization.A new report finds that generational wealth is enabling a record number of first-time homebuyers to pay in cash, increasing the gap between buyers and those priced out. The median age of first-time buyers also remains at a record high of 40.Herbert Blomstedt, a Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him lead many of the world's major orchestras, died this week at home. He was 99.   
   This newsletter was edited by Dorine Bethea.

title: How North Carolina Democrats flipped several House seats in historically GOP districts
body:
Supporters watch Democratic senatorial candidate Roy Cooper speak during an election night event in Raleigh, N.C. on November 3, 2026.
                
                    A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        A.M STEWART/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.   Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.   As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.   
   Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included:   High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.   
   North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.   One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.   He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.   
   "When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.   The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.   
   That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.   Yet as of Thursday, Davis was leading Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout by more than 10,000 votes. That's a larger margin than he won by in 2024.   North Carolina's 3rd Congressional District is one of five in the state that remain uncalled, with incumbent Republican Greg Murphy leading Democrat Raymond Smith by just 233 votes in a district where Democrats didn't even run a candidate in 2024. That race is likely headed for a recount.   In the 5th Congressional District, Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard is leading 11-term Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 99 votes — that's another race that may go to a recount.   If all of the remaining results hold, the state's congressional delegation would flip from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to 10 Democrats and four Republicans.
